53.text:
## Background
Isaiah 53 belongs to the second half of the book of Isaiah. Tradition credits the whole book to Isaiah son of Amoz, who preached in Jerusalem around 740 to 680 BC. Many scholars think chapters 40 to 55 come from a later prophet in Isaiah's tradition, writing to Jewish exiles in Babylon in the 500s BC. Readers often call this passage the fourth "Servant Song." It actually begins at Isaiah 52:13 and runs to the end of chapter 53. The servant's identity has long been debated. Jewish interpreters have often understood him as Israel, or a faithful remnant, suffering among the nations. Christians since the New Testament have read him as Jesus.

## What happens
The chapter opens with a startled question: who has believed this message, and to whom has God's power been shown (v. 1)? What follows is hard to believe. The servant grows up like a fragile shoot from dry ground, with nothing impressive about him (v. 2). People despise and reject him, and "we" turn our faces away (v. 3).

Then comes a turning point. The speakers realize they were wrong. They thought God was punishing him, but he was carrying their griefs and sorrows (v. 4). He was wounded for their wrongdoing, and his wounds bring their healing and peace (v. 5). Like wandering sheep, everyone went their own way, and the Lord laid their guilt on him (v. 6).

Verses 7–9 describe his silent suffering. Like a lamb led to slaughter, he does not protest (v. 7). He is taken away by an unjust judgment and cut off from the living for his people's sin (v. 8). Though he did no violence and spoke no deceit, he is buried among the wicked (v. 9).

The last verses look past his death. It was the Lord's will that he suffer, and his life becomes an offering for sin (v. 10). Yet he will "see his seed" and "prolong his days," words that point to life beyond death. God himself now speaks of "my righteous servant," who will make many righteous by bearing their iniquities (v. 11). God will give him a place among the great, because he poured out his life, was counted among sinners, carried their sin and prayed for them (v. 12).

## Key words and ideas
- The arm of the Lord: a picture of God's strength in action. The surprise is that God's power shows up in a weak, rejected servant.
- Griefs and sorrows: the Hebrew words can also mean sicknesses and pains. That is why the chapter speaks of healing as well as forgiveness.
- Offering for sin: verse 10 uses the word for the guilt offering in Israel's sacrifices. The servant's life does what those offerings did, making things right between God and people.
- Justify: to declare or make righteous. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians explain how this happens somewhat differently, but all read verse 11 as God's gift through the servant.

## Connections
John 12:38 quotes verse 1 to explain why many did not believe in Jesus despite his signs. Matthew 8:17 applies verse 4 to Jesus healing the sick. 1 Peter 2:24–25 echoes verses 5–6: "by whose stripes ye were healed," and the straying sheep now returned to their Shepherd. In Acts 8:32–33, an Ethiopian official is reading verses 7–8 and asks whom the prophet means, and Philip tells him about Jesus. 2 Corinthians 5:21 sums up the chapter's exchange: the one who knew no sin was made sin for us. Christian traditions put different emphasis on how this exchange works, whether as bearing punishment, offering sacrifice, or healing and defeating sin, but all draw on this chapter.

## For reflection
- The speakers admit they misjudged the servant. Whom might you be quick to see as "stricken" or deserving their trouble?
- What does it mean to you that the servant suffered in silence, without striking back?
- Verse 6 says "we have turned every one to his own way." Where do you notice yourself wandering, and what would returning look like?
